sweep_summary: Pirahã is in the catalog as 'weight' on the strength of Everett's 1983 UNICAMP thesis (Portuguese; syllable-type inventory). All six works with stress in the title are by Daniel or Keren Everett and all are about Pirahã word stress; two Glottolog records (692793 and 97410) are the same K. Everett 1998 acoustic-correlates article, one misattributed to Daniel. None of the six could be opened directly (NLLT 1988 paywalled at Springer; LI 1984 on JSTOR; WCCFL 3, JAL 1998 and the 1981 GEL proceedings print-only; But the 1986 SIL-UND Work Papers precursor of the NLLT 1988 paper was downloaded from archive.org (ERIC microfiche, 30 pp.) and read: it states the rule explicitly (rightmost token of the heaviest syllable type, scale CVV>GVV>VV>CV>GV, confined to the final three syllables; formalized as a right-edge amphibrach). Green 1995 (ROA-45) was also downloaded and restates the same rule citing Everett & Everett 1984 and Everett 1988. Together with Everett 1985 (BLS 11, already held by the project) these confirm the 'weight' coding; the 1986 statement is proposed as the new deciding quotation (English, explicit rule) over the 1983 thesis excerpt. Remaining acquisitions of medium priority: NLLT 1988 (for citation), LI 1984, K. Everett 1998.

new_statements.reading: Pirahã word stress is weight-sensitive and unbounded within a right-edge three-syllable window: the heaviest syllable type among the last three syllables is stressed, the rightmost of them on a tie, with a five-way weight scale in which a voiceless onset counts more than a voiced one (CVV > GVV > VV > CV > GV). Everett formalizes this as a ternary (amphibrach) foot at the right margin with obligatory branching. This is the same rule Everett 1985 (BLS 11, already held by the project) states in one sentence ('Stress the rightmost token of the heaviest syllable type within the final three syllables of the word'). The catalog's 'weight' coding is confirmed.

new_statements.relation_note: Wrong item for the listed citation (Everett 1986 Handbook grammar), which remains unopened; archive.org advancedsearch finds no open copy of Handbook vol. 1 beyond Rosetta Project excerpts for Canela-Krahô and Yagua. The item actually at the URL, Everett 2005 CA, is about Pirahã and its one prosody sentence (five-way syllable weight distinction, two tones) is consistent with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and with the existing Everett 1986 SIL-UND statement; it is a summary that cites those same works, not independent evidence, hence low confidence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The 2005 article gives no placement rule; it only says that Pirahã prosody rests on a five-way syllable-weight distinction (citing Everett 1979, 1988 and Everett & Everett 1984 for the details) and that the language has two tones (high vs. low). The placement rule itself (stress the heaviest syllable among the last three, rightmost on a tie, scale CVV > GVV > VV > CV > GV) is in the cited works, already held by the project.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the article does not discuss stress placement. It notes (p. 627 n. 11) that Sheldon analysed Pirahã with three underlying tones versus Everett's two.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern Pirahã proper (Everett's Maici river fieldwork); no dialect is named. Work 0's listed open copy is the wrong item: the archive.org identifier resolves to Everett 2005, Current Anthropology 46(4): 621-646, not the 1986 Handbook of Amazonian Languages grammar, which was not opened and for which no open copy was found on archive.org.

Revista Linguíʃtica (Programa de Pós-Graduação em Linguística, UFRJ) 10(2) [número 'Estudos de Línguas Indígenas', dezembro 2014]. DOI 10.31513/linguistica.2014.v10n2a4599.
tone_statements.quote: De acordo com D. Everett (1979) apud K. Everett (1998, p.108) Pirahã tem dois tons fonológicos, L (baixo) e H (alto), que são realizados em quatro padrões tonais possíveis: H, L, LH e HL. Sequências ascendentes e descendentes são interpretadas como sequências de tons nivelados. Apresentamos evidências preliminares de que Pirahã em seu atual estágio tem quatro tons: baixo, alto, ascendente e descendente distribuídos em dois registros, [+stiff] and [-stiff] (Bao, 1999), com tons ascendentes e descendentes interpretados como unidades. Seus alotons são codificados pelos traços [+slack] e [-slack].
tone_statements.translation: According to D. Everett (1979) apud K. Everett (1998: 108) Pirahã has two phonological tones, L (low) and H (high), realised in four possible tone patterns: H, L, LH and HL. Rising and falling sequences are interpreted as sequences of level tones. We present preliminary evidence that Pirahã at its present stage has four tones: low, high, rising and falling, distributed over two registers, [+stiff] and [-stiff] (Bao 1999), with rising and falling tones interpreted as units. Their allotones are encoded by the features [+slack] and [-slack].

tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone on nouns: traditional analysis two level tones H/L (mora-based, contours as sequences); author argues for four tones (L, H, rising, falling) organised in two registers, contours unitary; based on pitch measurements of nouns in isolation.

sources.note: First-hand, English, pre-publication version of the NLLT 1988 paper. Stress falls on the rightmost token of the heaviest syllable type (CVV>GVV>VV>CV>GV; voiceless onsets make a syllable heavier than voiced ones) within the last three syllables of the word; formalized as a right-edge amphibrach (ternary foot) with obligatory branching defaulting to rightmost; lexical compounds and extrametrical suffixes discussed. weight-sensitive, three-syllable window: confirms 'weight'.

sources.quote: Five syllable types CVV, GVV, VV, CV, GV distinguished by onset voicing; 'a acentuação depende primeiramente no tipo de sílaba e secundariamente da posição linear da sílaba'; rule: 'A acentuação recai na sílaba mais perto da última cuja duração, em termos de moras, não é superada por qualquer outra sílaba na palavra' (V = 1 mora, C = 3/4, G = 1/2). Earlier formulation without the explicit three-syllable window (diagram ranks final/penult/antepenult positions).

sources.citation: Green, Thomas. 1995. The stress window in Pirahã: a reanalysis of rhythm in Optimality Theory. MIT ms., Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-45, 26 pp. [not in the list of works with stress in the title; found during this search of works with stress in the title; secondary source]
sources.quote: The location of word stress in Pirahã (as described in Everett and Everett 1984, and Everett 1988) is a prime example of a word-final three-syllable window effect. In this language, the stress seeks out the heaviest of the last three syllables. In the event of a tie, stress occurs on the rightmost of the heaviest syllable type. If the window contains only light syllables, then again the rightmost receives the stress.
sources.note: Secondary (OT reanalysis relying on Everett's data), but a clean one-paragraph statement of the rule and of what the LI 1984 and NLLT 1988 papers describe. Confirms 'weight'.
